This is achieved by employing a transformer-based encoder-decoder architecture, which is trained to reconstruct the re-masked values. The authors argue that this method encourages the model to learn missingness-invariant representations, which are intended to be robust to missing data patterns. The paper presents a comprehensive empirical evaluation of ReMasker on 12 benchmark datasets, comparing its performance against 13 state-of-the-art imputation methods. The results demonstrate that ReMasker achieves competitive performance in terms of both imputation accuracy and utility. The authors also conduct extensive ablation studies to analyze the impact of various components of ReMasker, such as the masking ratio and embedding width. The paper also includes a theoretical justification for the method, arguing that the re-masking approach naturally accounts for missing values and encourages learning high-level representations beyond low-level statistics. Overall, the paper presents a well-motivated and empirically validated approach to missing value imputation, leveraging the power of masked autoencoding in a novel way. The authors successfully demonstrate the effectiveness of their method across a range of datasets and missingness scenarios, making a valuable contribution to the field of tabular data analysis.

The use of a transformer-based architecture further enhances the method's performance, leveraging the power of self-attention to capture complex relationships within the data. Third, the ablation studies are well-designed and provide valuable insights into the impact of different components of ReMasker. The analysis of the masking ratio and embedding width helps to understand the sensitivity of the method to these parameters and provides guidance for practical applications.
